details: The stated differentiation steps formally give p_tt + K ∂t(∂x u) = 0 and ∂x(∂t u) + (1/ρ)p_xx = 0; these displayed intermediate formulas are analyst expansions of the source's instructions [printed page 3, paragraph after (1.7); printed page 2, equation (1.5)].

Commuting the mixed derivatives and eliminating them gives p_tt = (K/ρ)p_xx; identifying K/ρ with c² yields the displayed result in the intended real sound-speed setting [printed page 3, mixed-derivative elimination explanation and (1.7); printed page 2, c = √(K/ρ)].

The conclusion is specifically an equation for pressure p; velocity u supplies the coupled auxiliary field in the antecedent acoustic system [printed pages 2–3, (1.5), (1.7), and the words 'equation for the pressure'].

The source separately defines first-order system hyperbolicity through real eigenvalues and a full set of independent eigenvectors; the classification assertion after (1.7) explicitly concerns the second-order equation [printed page 3, opening paragraph and paragraph after (1.7)].

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional constant-coefficient acoustic system p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/ρ)p_x = 0, with p the pressure perturbation, u the particle velocity, and c = √(K/ρ) the sound speed, the pressure satisfies p_tt = c² p_xx [printed page 2, equation (1.5) and definitions; printed page 3, equation (1.7)]. The source derives this by differentiating the first acoustic equation in time and the second in space and eliminating mixed derivatives of velocity, implicitly requiring sufficient regularity [printed page 3, paragraph after (1.7)]. It also calls the resulting second-order equation hyperbolic; exact regularity and parameter inequalities are left implicit in the physical context [printed pages 2–3, material definitions and classification paragraph after (1.7)].
